analysis.one_liner: Cuts taxes and rolls back regulation for community banks with assets under $10 billion.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 91 cosponsors from both parties and held one subcommittee hearing, but never received a committee markup or a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut federal taxes for banks and bank holding companies with $10 billion or less in assets, let them file shortened quarterly reports, exempted the smallest from some accounting rules, and loosened parts of the 2010 Dodd-Frank law for them. It would also have let a council of regulators veto Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rules on a lower threshold, and stripped the Fed's power to have the CFPB examine banks directly. A handful of provisions would have helped individual savers, such as new tax-favored accounts for children and tax deferral on long-term certificates of deposit.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners, executives, and shareholders of community banks come out best: a tax cut of up to $250,000 per C-corporation bank (up to $500,000 in distressed areas), a 20% pass-through reduction for banks organized as S corporations, an election to be taxed as partnerships, and a five-year loss carryback. The bill also grants tax-free treatment to interest banks earn on loans secured by agricultural real estate, and exempts smaller banks from several reporting, privacy-notice, and data-collection rules. Individual savers get smaller benefits: Roth-style 'young savers' accounts for people under 26, tax deferral and capital-gains-rate treatment on long-term CDs, and a higher small-issue bond cap that helps municipal issuers.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the aggregate federal tax of a community bank organized as a C corporation by 20% (up to $250,000), and by 50% (up to $500,000) for banks in empowerment zones, low-income, or other distressed areas; S-corporation banks get a similar pass-through reduction.

Lets community banks file a 'short form' quarterly report of condition in two nonsequential quarters each year and exempts banks with $1 billion or less in assets from the Sarbanes-Oxley internal-controls assessment.

Excludes from the bank's gross income the interest it earns on loans secured by agricultural real estate, and lets FDIC-insured institutions with $10 billion or less in assets elect partnership (LLC) tax treatment.

Creates tax-favored Roth 'young savers' accounts for children under 26, defers tax on interest from long-term nonnegotiable CDs while treating that interest at capital-gains rates, and triples the cap on qualified small-issue bonds from $10 million to $30 million.

Exempts loans held by creditors with $10 billion or less in assets from Dodd-Frank's escrow requirement on first-lien home loans, and lets state-licensed institutions with unchanged privacy practices skip the annual Gramm-Leach-Bliley privacy notice.

Lets the Financial Stability Oversight Council set aside any CFPB final rule that is 'inconsistent with the safe and sound operation' of financial institutions or that 'could adversely impact a subset of the banking industry disproportionately,' a much lower bar than the existing stability-of-the-system standard, and repeals the Federal Reserve's authority to delegate bank-examination powers to the CFPB.
Exempts banks with $1 billion or less in assets from the Equal Credit Opportunity Act's small-business lending data-collection requirements.

Lets banks amortize loan write-downs over ten years for capital purposes and average real estate appraisals over five years, softening the hit that the post-2008 property crash took on their regulatory capital.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers pay through the lost revenue from the bank tax cuts, the tax exclusion for interest on agricultural real estate loans, the CD and young-savers provisions, and the loss-carryback. Consumers who borrow from smaller banks lose some protections: escrow accounts for first-lien mortgages, the annual privacy notice, and small-business lending data collection would no longer apply to the smaller institutions. Regulators and the CFPB lose oversight tools, and bank capital measured with 10-year loss amortization and 5-year appraisal averaging would look stronger than the underlying losses really are, a risk borne by the deposit insurance fund if a bank later fails.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and borrowers at smaller banks

drawbacks.text: The Financial Stability Oversight Council veto over CFPB rules would apply whenever a rule 'could adversely impact a subset of the banking industry disproportionately' — a standard broad enough that almost any binding consumer rule affects some banks more than others, effectively giving the industry a standing veto over consumer regulation.

Allowing ten-year amortization of loan losses and five-year averaging of property appraisals in capital calculations can make a weak bank look healthy on paper, which regulators generally count as a safety-and-soundness risk to depositors and the deposit insurance fund.

The tax provisions — a bank income-tax cut, tax-free interest on agricultural real estate loans, partnership taxation for banks, and a five-year loss carryback — are permanent revenue losses to the Treasury, and the agricultural-interest exclusion is an open-ended subsidy to banks rather than a targeted program.
Weaker data-collection rules under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act for banks under $1 billion would make it harder to detect discrimination in small-business lending by those institutions.

Some relief is hard to argue with — shorter call reports, a one-time instead of annual privacy notice when practices have not changed — but these are bundled in the same bill as the deeper Dodd-Frank and CFPB rollbacks, so the low-risk items ride along with the high-risk ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The compliance-relief items (shorter reports, privacy-notice and record-fee fixes) are modest and defensible for very small banks. But the bill's center of gravity is a package of permanent tax cuts for bank owners plus structural rollbacks of Dodd-Frank consumer oversight, including a low-bar veto over CFPB rules and looser capital accounting that can hide losses. Whatever local-lending benefits might flow to communities are speculative, while the consumer-protection and revenue costs are concrete. As drafted, the costs weigh heavier than the benefits for the general public.

outcome.mechanism: It sat with three House committees for twenty months — referred to subcommittees, with a single subcommittee hearing in November 2011 — and expired when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013 without ever being marked up or voted on.

narrative.text: Rep. Blaine Luetkemeyer introduced the bill on May 3, 2011, and it was referred to the Ways and Means, Financial Services, and Agriculture Committees.
It attracted 91 cosponsors — 68 Republicans and 23 Democrats — the kind of bipartisan count that usually signals momentum.
The committees referred it to subcommittees in May and June 2011, and the only action thereafter was one subcommittee hearing on November 16, 2011.
No full committee ever reported the bill and the House never voted on it; it died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so the status quo won: Dodd-Frank consumer protections and CFPB examination authority stayed intact, the Treasury kept the revenue the bill would have surrendered, and large banks gained no new advantage for smaller rivals. Community bank owners, the bill's main intended beneficiaries, came out with nothing — and no similar package cleared Congress that session either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: consumer rules and revenue preserved

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 68 Republicans and 23 Democrats — but no vote was ever taken, so the record shows no roll-call split on the bill itself.

industries.industry: Community banks and bank holding companies ($10 billion or less in assets)
industries.note: The bill hands this group a package of tax cuts (up to $500,000 per bank in distressed areas, tax-free agricultural-loan interest, partnership-tax election) and exempts them from escrow, privacy-notice, and data-collection rules. Local borrowers and depositors might benefit if lower compliance costs support lending, but they also bear the weaker consumer protections and the risk of loss-masking capital accounting.

industries.industry: Owners of closely held banks and other subchapter S corporations
industries.note: The bill doubles the S-corporation shareholder limit to 200, permits preferred stock issuances, and allows IRA shareholders, expanding financing options for closely held firms. The cost is forgone Treasury revenue rather than a direct hit to consumers.

Every relief threshold in the bill is set at or below $10 billion, so large banks get nothing while smaller competitors gain tax and regulatory headroom — a relative competitive disadvantage, though no direct obligation is imposed on them.

industries.industry: Rural lenders in USDA guaranteed loan programs
industries.note: The bill authorizes a one-time fee of up to 1% on guaranteed rural business loans under $5 million and creates a preferred certified lender program, streamlining access to guarantees. Borrowers in rural communities may benefit from easier credit, but taxpayers backstop the guarantees.
